asDecan.p: Your Sun falls somewhere between ten and nineteen degrees of Sagittarius. Astrologers divide each sign into three ten-degree decans, and in the Golden Dawn order the middle one goes to the Moon, with the Nine of Wands as its card. Sagittarius is mutable fire under Jupiter, restless and hopeful. The Moon has no special dignity there, good or bad, so it takes on Jupiter's colouring and brings what it always brings, memory, mood, and a need for somewhere to come back to. That's a slightly odd set-up, since the Sun is the loud, public part of a chart and yours sits in the most private planet's ten degrees. Mercury's slice before you is all speed. Saturn's after you is where the load gets heavy. Yours is the sign at full strength with a few knocks already taken, like the man on the card with the bandage round his head, still gripping his staff. Temperance is the card for Sagittarius as a whole, and the Nine sits inside it.

You're the friend who says yes to the road trip and then quietly packs a first-aid kit, a spare charger and snacks for everyone. Sagittarius wants to go, and the Moon remembers what happened last time. At a family dinner you're warm and loud and telling stories, and you also clock the moment your sister goes quiet, and you'll bring it up with her later on the phone. When a plan you were excited about falls through, you're fine about it in public for a day or so. Then it catches up with you on a Tuesday night in the supermarket, standing in front of the cereal, and you're surprisingly low. Your mood follows your sense of whether life is going somewhere. With a trip booked, even a cheap weekend three months off, you'll put up with a lot of rubbish at work in the meantime.

You stay. Plenty of Sagittarians are brilliant for the first fortnight of someone's bad patch, and you're still ringing in month four, when a friend's divorce has gone dull and everyone else has stopped asking. The Moon keeps track of people, so you'll remember the anniversary of someone's dad dying without writing it down anywhere. The other thing, which people mostly find out by travelling with you, is how fast you make a strange place feel lived in. That's the Moon wanting a base, in a sign that's rarely in one place for long. Put you in a hostel dorm, a hospital waiting room, a friend's first flat with nothing in it yet, and within the hour you've found the kettle, sorted out who's sleeping where and tracked down a decent bakery, and everyone else is a bit less on edge without knowing why.

What people don't see straight away is how long you hold on to things. You'll forgive someone properly, you mean it, and then two years later in an argument about the dishes, out comes the thing they said at your birthday, word for word. The Moon files everything. The other habit is leaving early. If a job or a friendship starts to feel like it might hurt, you're often the one who goes first, handing in the notice or letting their messages sit on read, and you'll call it needing space. Sometimes it is. Sometimes you've just decided to go before anyone can make you, and I've seen people with this decan walk out of a job they liked the week after one bad review. The friends you've drifted from this way usually never knew anything was wrong.

When something goes badly, a redundancy, a break-up, a friend who lets you down, the first thing you do is get busy being fine. You make jokes about it at the pub and start looking at flights. That lasts a few days. About a week later it drops on you, usually at night, and you're lying awake going over every hard thing that's ever happened to you, right back to school. You can get prickly around then, short with your partner, cagey on the phone with your mum, and they're left guessing because a week ago you seemed okay. What helps is plain and physical. Proper sleep, a meal someone else cooked, and one person you tell the true version to early, before the jokes set in.

You come across as easygoing in love, up for anything, happy to split the bill and see where the night goes. Underneath that you're checking whether this person is safe to come home to. You'll want room to go off, a weekend hiking with friends, a month working abroad, and while you're away you miss them more than you let on, sending a photo of a sunset at eleven at night. What hurts you most is being teased about the things you believe in. A partner can mock your cooking all they like, but laugh at the retreat you went on, or the book that changed your mind about something, and you'll go cold for the evening without quite saying why. Tell them which things are off limits. They can't guess.

Work has to mean something to you, and it has to feel like it's heading somewhere, or your energy drains within months. Fields that mix care with distance suit this decan well. Remote-area nursing, aid work, teaching adults, running tours, anything where you look after people who are a long way from home. You're good in the long middle stretch of a job, the second year of a contract when the novelty's gone and the results haven't shown up yet, and you're often the one who talks everyone else into keeping at it. The trouble is you end up carrying the team's mood as well as your own workload. In a restructure you're the one colleagues come to for a debrief in the car park, and you'll do it, and go home flat. Bring that up at your next review, with two or three examples, before it wears you out.

At twenty this decan is often restless and a bit bruised. You leave home early or badly, you travel on little money, and the first few big disappointments land hard because you honestly expected things to go well. The late twenties are usually when the guard goes up. A few losses in, plenty of people with this slice of Sagittarius get wary, quicker to leave and slower to let anyone help, and they'd still call themselves optimists. Somewhere in the mid-thirties that tends to ease. You've been through enough to stop being shocked by setbacks, and you still expect things to work out, only now you've got a record to back it up. The fifties are often kind to you. I've seen plenty of people with this decan become the older friend everyone rings in a crisis, partly because they've clearly had a few of their own and are still laughing.

Keep a short list on your phone with a boring name, like 'done'. Whenever you get through something hard, a bad stretch at work, a hospital visit, a row that got sorted out, add one line with the date. No commentary. When the next rough patch starts and your head begins pulling up every old hurt, open the list instead and read the last five lines. Then text one of the people who got you through one of them, just to say hello.
